title: Can gas supply keep pace with rising US power demand?
gist: Wood Mackenzie teaser for an ebook asking whether US gas supply can keep pace with power demand driven by data centres and large loads, which is reviving interest in gas-fired and behind-the-meter generation. It frames five questions for utilities: where power-sector gas demand emerges, whether supply grows in the right places, whether pipelines keep pace, how much LNG exports will compete, and what it means for regional gas prices and basis.

insights.claim: Data centres and other large loads are adding US electricity demand, and the need for firm capacity and faster access to power is supporting renewed interest in gas-fired generation, including behind-the-meter projects.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Behind-the-meter gas generation for data centres is a growth niche for turbine/engine OEMs and gas suppliers.
insights.quote: the need for firm capacity and faster access to power is supporting renewed interest in gas-fired generation, including behind-the-meter projects
insights.locator: What does rising US power demand mean for gas supply?

insights.claim: The location of new gas-fired and behind-the-meter generation matters alongside headline power-demand growth for assessing where power-sector gas demand will emerge.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Map gas demand at the node/regional level, not national totals, when sizing gas exposure from data centres.
insights.locator: Where is new power-sector gas demand emerging?

insights.claim: National US gas production forecasts alone may not reveal whether sufficient supply will reach individual demand centres.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Aggregate supply adequacy can coexist with local shortages; regional basis is where the mispricing shows up.
insights.quote: national production forecasts alone may not reveal whether sufficient supply will reach individual demand centres
insights.locator: Is gas supply growing in the right places?

insights.claim: Whether pipeline investment keeps pace with demand depends on project location, capacity, timing and likelihood of development, all of which determine future gas availability.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Risk-weight announced pipeline projects by development likelihood when forecasting regional gas deliverability.
insights.locator: Is pipeline investment keeping pace with demand?

insights.claim: Growing US LNG exports could compete with domestic power generation for regional gas supply and pipeline infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: LNG export buildout is a tightening factor for regional gas used by power generators.
insights.locator: How much gas demand will LNG exports create?

insights.claim: Regional gas price forecasts, basis relationships, infrastructure and supply-demand conditions are key context for gas-fired generation economics.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Spark-spread and power asset valuations should model regional basis explicitly rather than Henry Hub alone.
insights.locator: What could these changes mean for regional gas prices?

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie pitches Lens Gas & LNG to Lens Power & Renewables users as a way to view power demand, generation requirements and the underlying fuel market as one connected picture.
insights.speaker: Dulles Wang
insights.so_what: Indicates utilities are being sold integrated gas-power planning tools as the markets converge.
insights.locator: How can utilities connect their gas and power market outlooks?
